design: 2,040 B2B customers of a European logistics firm; treatment = salesperson change (relationship disruption) occurring in one of the four quarters of 2014 (680 treated, four adoption cohorts), compared with 1,360 randomly sampled never-disrupted customers assigned to the same quarters.
reason: Adoption is staggered across four quarters and binary, but every main-text model (Table 5 Models 0-2, Table 6 Models 3-4) is a two-period DiD on data collapsed to a 12-month pre period (T1) and 12-month post period (T2) relative to the disruption: disruption-group dummy + post dummy + interaction, with sampled-quarter/industry/region dummies, no customer fixed effects and no calendar-time fixed effects. The (b) columns add time-varying controls (visits, relative importance, portfolio breadth/complexity, sales growth rates); Table 6 adds moderator-by-treatment interactions. No unstacked panel TWFE or event study appears anywhere in the main text.
appendix_only_specs: Web Appendix reports common-trend checks, a Heckman/inverse-Mills correction, propensity-score-matched ATEs, and subsample splits; all described as the same two-period design, none a panel TWFE.
notes: Underlying data are monthly product-level transactions 2012-2015 (48 months), so a staggered panel could be built in principle, but the paper only reports the two-period collapse. Table 5 column (a) 'without controls' still has only group/post dummies plus quarter dummies, not unit FE.
data_statement: Proprietary transaction data from an unnamed central European B2B logistics company; no data or code availability statement; only an online supplement (Web Appendix) at the article DOI is mentioned.

design: Monthly car-model x country panel for 20 automotive brands in 9 countries (2000 to 2015); treatment is a collective layoff announcement by brand j in country c (205 announcements at different months), treated units are the brand's car models in the layoff country for 12 months after the announcement, controls are the same brand's models in other countries with no announcement within +/-12 months, stacked into 24-month event windows (129,919 observations).
reason: The DiD is embedded in a hierarchical Bayesian three-equation system (Equations 1 to 7): log sales is regressed on log advertising, log price, log competitive sales and lagged advertising with random car-model and time effects, and the Post x CLCountry interaction enters second-layer equations for the brand-country-time intercept and elasticities together with production capacity utilization (Table 3, Table 4). Advertising and price are instrumented with control-country averages (Equations 3 and 5), the windows are stacked per announcement (footnote 9, Web Appendix B), CLCountry is switched on only within the 24-month window, and Model 2 adds Domestic, MotiveD and Employees moderators. No main-text column reports a plain linear TWFE on the binary treatment without the time-varying marketing-mix controls, so every specification violates the protocol (stacked, time-varying controls, IV, nonlinear/hierarchical model, treatment-by-covariate interactions).
appendix_only_specs: Web Appendix C reports OLS, SUR and 2SLS versions of the sales equation and robustness to global capacity utilization, production-worker-only events and 18-month windows; these keep the stacked structure and the marketing-mix controls and are in any case appendix-only. Web Appendix B describes the stacking of the DiD variables.
notes: Treatment is staggered in calendar time (announcements spread over 2000 to 2015) and binary, but the estimand is defined in event windows with treatment switching off after 12 months; brand-country cells can be treated repeatedly. The headline sales effect (8.7 percent) is a simulated but-for comparison (Equations 9 to 12), not a regression coefficient. The posterior mean of Post x CLCountry on base sales in Table 3 is 1.45 [0.87, 2.15] but that intercept is conditional on the elasticity shifts and controls.
data_statement: No data or code availability statement; sales, price and production data were purchased from R.L. Polk Automotive (now IHS), advertising data from Nielsen, Kantar and Focus Media, layoff announcements were hand-collected, convergence plots are 'available on request', and the article points only to an online supplement at https://doi.org/10.1177/0022242919901277.

design: 21,096 packaged food/beverage products (9,083 brands, 4,408 firms) launched 2003-2011 in 44 U.S. categories from Mintel GNPD; treatment = first adoption of a Facts Up Front-style FOP label by any brand in the category (category-specific adoption dates, first-adopter brands dropped), FOP = 1 for all products in a treated category after that date; controls are 8 categories with no FOP adoption through 2011.
reason: Adoption is binary and staggered at the category level (the authors exploit 'temporal variation in adoption of FOP at the product category level' and correlate adoption timing with category healthiness across treated categories), with never-treated control categories, and the data are a repeated cross-section of product launches assigned to stable brand/firm/category units. But every main-text specification, Equation 1 and Table 2 columns 1-4 (coef .9490, SE .3713 in column 1) and Table 4 columns 1-7, includes category-specific linear time trends (plus a common linear trend alongside year FE), which is the protocol's unit-specific-trends exclusion since the category is the treated unit. Columns 2-4 of Table 2 additionally interact FOP with brand or category moderators. No column drops the category trends.
appendix_only_specs: Web Appendix Tables W3-W11 (alternative outcomes, moderators, brand-mortality sample, firms in both groups, alternative classification windows) and W12-W17 (parallel-trend interactions, placebo, fake treatment group, fake outcomes) are described as the same DD model; the text gives no indication that any drops the category-specific trends.
notes: Brand, firm, and category FE are all included additively (brands nest in firms, so firm FE is redundant; category FE is nonredundant only if brands span categories). Fixed effects are at the brand level while treatment varies at the category level, which is allowed. The data (Mintel GNPD) are commercial, so re-estimation would require a license.
data_statement: Data come from the commercial Mintel Global New Products Database with hand-coded FOP adoption from package photographs; no data or code availability statement, only an online supplement (Web Appendix) at the article DOI.

design: Units are Kantar France panel households (3,674 and 3,555 Leclerc; 2,224 and 7,667 Intermarche) observed over 91 four-week periods 2008-2014 in local markets where the retailer opened a click-and-collect point; treatment is a household-level step dummy (CCShopper) that turns on when the household starts repeat C&C shopping at the retailer, at household-specific dates; non-adopting and not-yet-adopting households in the same markets are the comparison.
reason: The CCShopper step dummy is a binary, household-specific staggered adoption with household and time fixed effects (Equation 1), so the design is in scope. But the only main-text regression table (Table 5, six columns: online, brick-and-mortar, and total spending for each retailer) always includes time-varying controls (counts of own and competing C&Cs, super/hypermarkets, independent retailers), a post-opening linear trend, a second step treatment (Type_Open for the local C&C opening), two control-function residuals from IV first stages (CF_Open, CF_CCShopper), the CCShopper x Type interaction, and seven time-invariant shopper characteristics interacted with CCShopper and with CCShopper x Type. No column reports a plain binary TWFE, and the table reports only coefficients with significance stars, no standard errors.
appendix_only_specs: Web Appendix W3: robustness checks including a two-period before/after collapse, a propensity-score-matched DiD, and a version using the local C&C opening (market-level staggered rollout) as the treatment; W4-A to W4-C re-estimate Equation 1 for total grocery spending, trips, and spending per trip across all retailers. All appear to retain the Equation 1 controls and control-function terms.
notes: Treatment is self-selected household adoption (endogenous timing), which the paper handles with control functions; the market-level C&C opening (Type_Open, 101 near-store and 82 stand-alone Leclerc markets, 66 in-store and 212 near-store Intermarche markets, openings before January 2014) is itself a staggered binary rollout but appears in the main text only as a control and in Web Appendix W3 as an alternative treatment. Table 5 CCShopper (a1) coefficients: online spending 36.04 (Intermarche), 42.73 (Leclerc); brick-and-mortar 39.46, 2.64; total 75.50, 45.37; all p<.01, no SEs printed. Moderators are measured in the year before the C&C opening. Published JM 2021, Vol. 85(4), 158-178.
data_statement: No data availability statement; the acknowledgment says the authors are indebted to AiMark for providing the Kantar France household panel data, complemented by Experian, A3Distrib, and INSEE data. An online supplement (web appendices W1-W5) is at the article DOI. No code or public repository mentioned.

design: Study 2: 107 propensity-score-matched product-recall events (2014 to 2018) of US public firms that handle complaints on Twitter, daily abnormal returns in a [-5, +5] event window (N = 1,177 = 107 x 11 days); treated units are firms using an open-exchange response strategy (>75 percent of complaints handled via multiple public exchanges), controls are matched closed-exchange firms hit by their own recall, and treatment is Open x Post-recall with recall dates differing across firms.
reason: Equation 7 (Y_it = b Open_i x Post_t + g X_it + a_i + y_t) is estimated on a matched sample built by nearest-neighbor propensity-score matching with replacement (Appendix B), and every main-text column (Table 3 Models 3.1 to 3.6, Table 4 Models 4.1 to 4.4) includes the 20-plus time-varying 'window-time controls' listed in the Table 3 notes (daily followers, complaint volume and valence, response timeliness, etc.). The panel is a pool of 11-day event windows with event-day fixed effects (Model 3.1 reports relative-time interactions with the event day as baseline), so the structure is stacked rather than calendar-time TWFE; Model 3.4 additionally drops firm fixed effects and Models 3.5, 3.6 and Table 4 add triple interactions. Study 1 (Table 2) is a quarterly control-function regression with continuous response volume, not a DiD.
appendix_only_specs: Web Appendix reports an interval plot of the Model 3.1 event study, a future-complaints DiD (also summarized in main-text Model 3.3), robustness to sample selection and extra controls for Study 1, and details of the publicity-ratio measure; none is reported without the time-varying controls or without matching.
notes: Borderline between near-miss and ineligible: the 'treatment' is a time-invariant firm strategy (open vs closed exchange) interacted with a post-recall indicator, and both treated and control firms experience a recall, so each matched pair is a 2x2 DiD and the staggering arises only because recall dates differ across pairs. I classify it as near-miss because treated units switch on at unit-specific calendar dates with never-treated controls, but a lead who reads the design as a pooled set of common-shock 2x2 comparisons could reasonably mark it ineligible. Violations: matching-based DiD, time-varying controls in all columns, event-time (stacked) fixed effects, triple interactions.
data_statement: No data or code availability statement; Twitter data were scraped by the authors and supplemented with a proprietary social-media dataset, financial data from Compustat, CRSP, YouGov, Ad$pender, RavenPack and 13-F filings, and one robustness result is said to be 'available upon request'; the article points only to an online supplement at https://doi.org/10.1177/00222429211002183.

design: Firm-year panel of ACSI-covered US firms, 1995-2017 (141 firms in the DiD sample, 204 in the conventional panel); binary treatment is engaging in M&A activity in a given year (SDC Platinum), which occurs at firm-specific years and recurs for many firms; comparison is firms with no M&A activity (plus matched control groups).
reason: M&A events happen in different calendar years for different firms with never-acquiring firms as controls, so the underlying design is staggered and binary, but no main-text specification is an unstacked TWFE with calendar-time fixed effects. The DiD in Eq. 2 / Table 5 is estimated on stacked four-year 'clean' rolling windows with a firm fixed-effects within estimator and a window-relative Post-M&A dummy (fourth year of each window) rather than calendar-year FE; Model 1 (no covariates) still has this stacked structure, Models 2-3 add lagged time-varying controls, and Models 4-5 use matched control groups. Table 3 (SUR) and Table 8 add controls, window-relative time effects and mediators; Table 6 uses a differenced CSAT outcome with controls and inverse-Mills-ratio selection terms.
appendix_only_specs: Web Appendix D (Tables D.1-D.5, Figures D.1-D.3) has the matching details, selection model and pre-trend comparisons for alternative control groups; Web Appendix F re-estimates the mediation system with an industry control and as a four-equation system. No calendar-FE TWFE reported there either, judging from the text.
notes: Table 5 Model 1 (firm FE, Post-M&A dummy, interaction only): M&A Group x Post-M&A = -.635 (SE .316, bootstrapped), Post-M&A = .467 (.114), N = 2,840 obs, 141 firms, 67 M&A firms. Treatment is a recurring yearly event, not an absorbing adoption; the clean-window rule excludes firms with M&As in adjacent years, and 153 of 204 panel firms acquire at some point, so the never-treated pool is small in the full panel. A calendar-FE TWFE on the raw firm-year M&A indicator would be possible in principle but is not reported.
data_statement: No data or code availability statement; data come from the ACSI database, Compustat, SDC Platinum, CRSP, S&P Capital IQ and EDGAR annual reports (licensed commercial sources), with the list of M&A firms and supplementary tables in the online Web Appendix at https://doi.org/10.1177/00222429211024255.

design: Units are category-store-week cells (47 categories x 285 Dutch generalist grocery stores, IRI weekly data 2012-2015); treatment is exposure to a premium organic specialist (Ekoplaza) store opening within 5 km, with three entry events (March 2013, March 2014, April 2014) treating 38 incumbent stores, versus 247 never-exposed control stores from the same five retailers, observed six months before and after each entry.
reason: Three entry dates and a binary exposure indicator with category-store and weekly fixed effects (Equation 2) make this a staggered binary design, but no main-text column satisfies the protocol. Table 4 and all five columns of Table 5 include time-varying controls (log paid price and log assortment size) plus Gaussian-copula endogeneity terms (dropped only in Model 4, which keeps the price and assortment controls), six pre-period organic-focus moderators interacted with Treatment x Post, Treatment x Post x Paid price, store-characteristic interactions, and inverse-probability-of-treatment weights estimated from trading-area covariates. The sample is also assembled event by event with each control store randomly assigned to one entry (footnote 6), a stacked structure.
appendix_only_specs: Web Appendix B (IPTW propensity model), C (placebo-treatment and pre-trend tests), F (category-level moderators). No unadjusted TWFE is reported there according to the main text.
notes: Footnote 7 reports that the parallel-trends test is rejected on the unweighted sample and passes only after IPTW weighting, so a plain unweighted TWFE re-estimation would be on a sample where the authors themselves reject pre-trends. Only three entry events, two of them one month apart. Table 4 Treatment x Post = -.033 (robust SE .003), N = 13,395 category-store cases x weeks (~52 weeks each); Table 5 columns: -.033, -.033, -.034, -.033, -.036 (no SEs printed in Table 5). Published JM 2023, Vol. 87(1), 97-113.
data_statement: No data availability statement; store-level scanner data are from IRI (Netherlands) with store locations from IRI and organic store opening dates from retailer websites and the business press. An online supplement (web appendices A-F) is at the article DOI. No code or public repository mentioned.

design: Physician-year panel of all Medicare Part B physicians, 2012-2015 (N = 3,473,954 physician-years); treatment = being rated on Yelp (Rated_j x Post_t switches on in the year of the physician's first Yelp review, which varies across physicians); comparison = never-rated physicians.
reason: The Rated_j x Post_t term in Equation 2 is a staggered binary adoption indicator with never-treated controls, and the paper says alpha is 'identified from variations across and within physicians in the timing of their first Yelp review'. However, every main-text specification (Table 2 columns 1-4, Table 4 columns 1-4, Table 5 columns 1-4, and the event study in Equation 6 / Figure 2) also includes the continuous, time-varying treatment-intensity regressor Rating_jt x Rated_j x Post_t (cumulative average star rating), which is the paper's key coefficient; columns 2 and 4 of each table instrument it with reviewer leniency (IV), and all models are weighted by inverse-probability-of-treatment propensity-score weights. Table 5 adds subgroup-by-treatment interactions and number-of-reviews fixed effects. No column reports Rated x Post alone.
appendix_only_specs: Web Appendix C (Tables W2, C2-C4), E, F referenced for first stage, pretrend-by-instrument, alternative instruments, lagged ratings, and fraudulent-review exclusion; all are variants of the same IV/continuous-rating model, none described as a clean binary TWFE.
notes: Fixed effects are physician FE plus specialty-by-year and HSA-by-year FE, which would be allowed on their own (time-invariant characteristics x calendar time). The disqualifying elements are the continuous Rating x Rated x Post regressor (treatment intensity) in every column, IV in half the columns, and IPTW propensity weighting (closer to matching-based DiD than to simple analysis weights). Physicians first rated before 2012 are always-treated within the 2012-2015 outcome window. Published JM 2024, 88(1), 77-96 despite the 2021 year tag in the batch.
data_statement: No data or code availability statement; Yelp data were scraped by the authors, Medicare research identifiable files are restricted-access CMS data, and the only pointer is the journal online supplement at https://doi.org/10.1177/00222429221146511.

design: Consumer-month panel from one Asian online retailer (36 months; 2,225 members and 3,129 nonmembers); binary treatment = enrollment in membership-based free shipping, switching on in the consumer's enrollment month, which varies across consumers over the 14 post-launch months; comparison group = propensity-score-matched consumers who never enrolled.
reason: The design is staggered and binary (the paper calls it a staggered treatment and cites Goodman-Bacon and Baker-Larcker-Wang), but every main-text specification is a stacked DiD (Eq. 2a/2b, 4, 5 with consumer-by-cohort and month-by-cohort fixed effects) estimated on a 1:1 propensity-score-matched sample and augmented with a control-function generalized residual from a probit first stage using a zip-code peer-enrollment instrument. Table 4 (average and dynamic effects on spending, frequency, order size, variety, impulse share, NCR), Table 5 and Table 6 (interactions with pre-enrollment characteristics), and Table 7 (churn, linear probability) all share this stacked + matched + control-function setup. The conventional TWFE-DiD is reported only in Table W10 of Web Appendix A, and the leads-lags event study only in Figure W3 of the web appendix.
appendix_only_specs: Web Appendix A Table W10: conventional TWFE-DiD (individual and month FE) and a version without the control-function residual, both apparently on the matched sample; Figure W3: leads-lags (-12..+12) event study with the stacked FE structure; Table W6: month-by-month dynamic effects; Table W11: Cox hazard for churn.
notes: Three independent disqualifiers in the main text: stacked DiD, PSM matching, and control-function/IV residual. Treatment lasts 12 months and can expire (membership not renewed), so treatment may switch off for some consumers in extended samples (Table W9). Table 4 headline: Enroll coefficient on log spending .05 (.04) n.s.; NCR .12 (.04). Robust (not clustered) SEs.
data_statement: Proprietary order-level transaction data provided by an unnamed top online retailer in Asia; no data or code availability statement; an online supplement (web appendix) is at https://doi.org/10.1177/00222429231158116.

design: MarketScan 2011-2012 claims for 2,282 patients with a single LDL test at exactly 129 mg/dL (control) or 130 mg/dL (treated, 'bad news'); treatment switches on at each patient's own test date, which is spread roughly uniformly over 2011-2012; outcomes are drug purchases per 30-day window and generic-vs-brand choice per transaction, with a secondary A1c sample (6.9% vs 7%).
reason: Patients receive the bad-news treatment at patient-specific calendar dates and the 129 mg/dL patients serve as an untreated comparison group, so the design is binary and staggered in calendar time. However, every main-text specification (Eq. 1-2; Table 2 cols 1-6; Tables 3 and 5) defines time as 30-day windows relative to each patient's own test date and uses relative-time (event-time) fixed effects instead of calendar-time fixed effects, which the protocol requires; the generic-choice regressions (Table 2 cols 3-6, Tables 3, 5) additionally include molecule fixed effects and are transaction-level linear probability models, and cols 4-6 / Tables 3, 5 add subgroup-by-treatment interactions or sample splits.
appendix_only_specs: Web Appendix B reports placebo thresholds and placebo test dates and a formal pre-trend test; Web Appendix C the new-molecule adoption analysis; Web Appendix D multiple testers; Web Appendix E class-specific estimates; Web Appendix F out-of-pocket price version. None uses calendar-time FE as described.
notes: Identification is an RD-style local randomization at the 129/130 threshold combined with a before/after comparison; the control group also experiences the test event at its own date, so 'Post' is defined for both groups. Table 2 col 1 (log purchases): Treated x Post = .0171 (SE .0176), individual FE + relative-period FE, N = 31,567; col 3 (generic LPM): -.0109 (.0064) with molecule FE, N = 34,935. If the lead treats event-time FE as acceptable, col 1 and col 2 would be the only controls-free, molecule-FE-free candidates, but they still lack calendar-time FE.
data_statement: No data or code availability statement; the data are proprietary MarketScan commercial claims (including Lab files) plus average wholesale price data, and supplementary analyses are in the online Web Appendix at https://doi.org/10.1177/00222429231158360.

design: 2,693 U.S. publicly listed firms (30,679 firm-years, 1986-2018); treatment = universal demand (UD) law adoption in the firm's state of incorporation, staggered across 25 states from Georgia 1989 to Louisiana 2015; controls are firms incorporated in states that never adopt or have not yet adopted.
reason: The design is a classic staggered binary state-law DiD with never-treated controls (Web Appendix A lists adoption years). However, every main-text specification (Table 5 parallel-trends model; Table 6 columns 1-5, Equations 1-2) is a conditional logit (fixed-effects logit) with year FE and two-digit SIC industry FE; the authors state explicitly that firm fixed effects cannot be included because never-recalling firms have no within-firm variation in the binary outcome. The logit functional form rules every column out, and columns 2-5 also carry lagged time-varying controls (SLACK, SIZE, LEVERAGE, ROA, R&D intensity, INST_OWNERSHIP, ENTRENCHMENT) and, in columns 3-5, moderator-by-treatment interactions. Table 6 column 1 (no controls, z = -2.32 on UD_LAW x POST_ADOPTION = -.7467) would otherwise be the cleanest spec but is still a logit with industry rather than firm FE.
appendix_only_specs: Web Appendix E (recalls with prior injury/death), F (subperiods), G (ordered logit on recall counts), H (recall timing), I (operational-improvement controls, Table W9), J (dropping top-3 recall firms, Table W10); all are logit/ordered-logit variants of the same industry-FE specification, no linear TWFE.
notes: Outcome is a firm-year binary recall indicator; a linear probability TWFE re-estimation with firm FE is feasible in principle from the described data (Compustat + CPSC + state of incorporation), but the paper reports no linear model anywhere. Table 5 adds relative-time pre-adoption indicators (-3, -2, -1) interacted with UD_LAW, but again inside a logit.
data_statement: Data come from Compustat, CPSC recall and Safer Products websites, EDGAR 10-K filings, Thomson Reuters 13F, and ISS; no data or code repository is named, only a Web Appendix (online supplement at the article DOI) and 'results available upon request' for one robustness check.

design: 250,055 JD.com customers across 416 Chinese cities observed monthly over roughly 10 years; treatment = living in a city where JD launched its own delivery service (ODS), described as launched in April 2010 in nine cities, with 16 ODS cities in the analysis; controls are customers in cities that kept third-party delivery.
reason: The article models a single launch: After is defined as 'whether period t is before (= 0) or after (= 1) the ODS launch' and the only date given is April 2010, so as written the design is a one-date treated/control comparison rather than a documented staggered rollout. Even setting that aside, every main-text regression (Table 4 common-trend test, Table 5 Equation 2, Table 6 Equation 3, Table 9 Equation 5, Table 10 Equations 6-8) is estimated on a propensity-score-matched sample, adds a Heckman inverse Mills ratio, includes time-varying customer controls (recency, relationship length, largest order size, cumulative spending) and city/company controls, uses an ODS group dummy instead of customer fixed effects, and replaces calendar-time FE with a linear Month trend plus 11 seasonal month dummies. The city-level analysis (Tables 7-8, Figures 2-4) is synthetic control.
appendix_only_specs: Web Appendix D reports DID without matching, Poisson DID, alternative matching, trimmed sample, hierarchical linear model and a redefined treatment (Tables W3-W8); Appendix C has event-time coefficient plots (Figures W5-W7); Appendix E/F/G robustness for heterogeneity and mediation. None is described as a TWFE with customer and calendar-month FE.
notes: Ambiguity flagged for the lead: 16 ODS cities and the phrase 'initial rollout of ODS from 2010 through 2013' suggest the real-world rollout was staggered, and After and Aftermonth carry an i subscript in Equations 2-3, but the article never lists city-specific launch dates and defines After as a single post indicator. If the lead has evidence of distinct city launch dates, reclassify as near-miss (matching-based, Heckman correction, time-varying controls, no unit or calendar-time FE); the eligible set is unaffected either way. Main coefficient for reference: Table 5 ODS x After on log spending = .078 (SE .007), N = 3,096,012.
data_statement: Proprietary customer transaction and review data obtained from JD.com; no data or code availability statement; only a Web Appendix (online supplement at the article DOI) and instructor slides on the AMA website are mentioned.

design: Study 1: consumer-level snack calorie data for 474 panelists observed one day before and one day after the spring onset of daylight saving time (rolling two-week panels, 2004-2010), treated = residents of six DST-observing states near Arizona, control = Arizona residents; Study 2: 4,273 fitness-center members observed one week before and one week after one year's DST onset, treated = California, control = Arizona/Hawaii.
reason: Treatment is the switch to daylight saving time, a single policy date common to all treated consumers in a given year; each cohort is observed only in a pre/post window around that one date and cohorts from different years do not overlap in calendar time, so the design is a pooled two-period (2x2) DiD with a never-treated control, not a staggered-adoption panel (Eq. 1, Table 4 col 1; Table 5 fall transition; Table 7 five- and seven-day windows). Study 2 (Eq. 4, Table 11) is a fixed-effects Poisson model around one date and would be excluded as nonlinear in any case. No unit adopts while other units remain not-yet-treated in the same calendar period.
appendix_only_specs: Web Appendices D-N contain parallel-trend plots, Sunday placebo tests, fake-treatment-group bootstraps, expanded treated-state lists, ounces as DV, variety-seeking controls, a no-consumer-FE version with controls, and a visit-choice (binary) version of Study 2; none changes the single-date design.
notes: Formally, the second Sunday of March falls on a different calendar date each year, so a lead could read the pooled 2004-2010 sample as having multiple 'adoption dates'; but each consumer is observed around exactly one event and no cross-cohort comparisons exist, so TWFE collapses to the simple DiD (Table 4 col 1: DST = 210.622, SE 48.729, individual FE + time FE, N = 1,307). If the lead prefers to classify this as a staggered design, the verdict would be near-miss for two-period collapse rather than eligible.
data_statement: No data or code availability statement; both datasets come from anonymous providers (a multinational packaged-food firm's consumer panel and a national fitness-center chain) under confidentiality agreements, supplementary analyses are in the online supplement at https://doi.org/10.1177/00222429241256570.

design: Units are 2,625 independent toy retailers; treatment is the supplier's launch of its own web shop in the retailer's country (France June 2017, United Kingdom July 2017), with Spanish retailers (no launch) as controls; outcomes are ordering-strategy components aggregated to one before and one after observation per retailer.
reason: Study 1a is a binary treatment with two country-level adoption dates one month apart and an untreated control country, so it is formally staggered, but every main-text specification violates the protocol. Equation 1 (Table 3) and Equation 2 (Table 5) collapse the data to two periods per retailer (before/after, matched to the same calendar months a year earlier), use retailer random effects rather than fixed effects, and have no calendar-time fixed effects beyond a single After dummy; Table 5 adds moderator-by-treatment interactions. Table 4 robustness columns use nearest-neighbor matching (cols 1, 5), a quarterly panel with matching and a seasonal control (col 5), or a country dummy (col 6), none of which is a plain TWFE. Study 1b is a matched change model and Study 2 is a scenario experiment.
appendix_only_specs: Web Appendix D: placebo event one year earlier (Table WD.3), alternative moderator operationalizations (WD.4, WD.5), details of the quarterly matched panel (WD.1) and country-control model (WD.2). None is a plain staggered TWFE.
notes: The staggering is minimal: only two treated cohorts (France, UK) whose launch dates differ by one month, and the analysis aligns both into a single before/after contrast (Spain's periods defined by the France date; footnote 7 says results are robust to using the UK date). A reader who requires calendar-date variation that the regression actually exploits could call this ineligible as effectively a single-event two-group design. Table 3 Treatment x After: distinct SKUs -.380 (.118), quantity/SKU -.038 (.039), wholesale price .250 (.115), order value -.166 (.081); N = 5,250 (4,876 for price). Dependent variables are normalized by their initialization-period value.
data_statement: No data availability statement; the transactional data come from a confidential German toy supplier whose name cannot be revealed (footnote 3), and an online supplement (web appendices) is at the article DOI. No code or public repository mentioned.

design: Customer-week panel (52 weeks, Apr 2020-Apr 2021) at an anonymous US apparel retailer; treatment is a customer's adoption of BNPL installment payments, switching on at the customer's own adoption week within the four weeks after the retailer's October 2020 launch (up to four weekly adoption cohorts, adoption week itself dropped); comparison is 25,000 never-adopting customers matched 1:1 on pre-period behavior.
reason: Equation 1 is a TWFE regression of outcomes on a unit-specific post-adoption step dummy with customer and week fixed effects and no controls, and footnote 8 acknowledges within-month variation in treatment timing, so the design is staggered and binary. But every main-text specification (Table 5, Table 6) is estimated on the Mahalanobis-matched adopter/nonadopter sample, which the protocol excludes as matching-based DiD; the purchase incidence column is a logit (nonlinear), and Table 6 adds subgroup-by-treatment interactions. The unmatched version using all 200,000 nonadopters is only reported in Web Appendix B.

design: Units are NielsenIQ Homescan households observed annually 2004-2019 (9,411 households, 93,300 household-years); treatment is a binary indicator for having an at-home internet connection, which switches on at household-specific adoption years (average adoption year 2010); the sample keeps only households that adopt during the panel, so not-yet-treated households are the comparison group.
reason: Equation 3 (Table 3, HHD-TWFE) regresses six household outcomes on the binary at-home-internet indicator with household and year fixed effects only, no controls, standard errors clustered by household; adoption is staggered across 2004-2019 with many cohorts and not-yet-treated households serve as controls, satisfying every protocol rule. Table 4 reports a de Chaisemartin-d'Haultfoeuille (2024) heterogeneous-DID estimate of the same design with pretrend and dynamics tests (Figure 6 event study); that estimator is not on the protocol's accepted list, but footnote 11 states Callaway-Sant'Anna gives very similar results (numbers not reported). design: Daily product-level panel on three Amazon marketplaces (May 2020 to Jan 2021); Study 1 regresses organic search visibility on an indicator for Amazon holding the buy box that switches on and off repeatedly (buy box seller changes about every 82 hours), Study 2 compares Amazon Basics products with matched third-party products using a time-invariant first-party indicator within comparison-group fixed effects.
reason: There is no staggered adoption: the Study 1 first-party indicator isAmazonBuyBox (Equation 7, Table 4) is a high-frequency switching state rather than an adoption event, and the Study 2 indicator isAmazonBasics (Equation 8, Table 6) is time-invariant, so delta is a cross-sectional contrast within comparison groups. Both main models are two-way fixed effects Poisson (log-link GLM) with time-varying controls (log sales rank, log price, log review count, product rating, seller rating, isPrime). The specification curve (Figures 6 to 8) varies OLS vs Poisson and fixed-effect sets but never defines an adoption design, so no DiD specification exists to qualify.
appendix_only_specs: Web Appendix C reports an outcome-based (OB) test with sales rank as the outcome using the same switching indicator; Web Appendices D to F report specification-curve details, comparison-group exclusions and omitted-variable sensitivity. None is a staggered DiD.
notes: Conceptual-plus-measurement paper; the authors call the models two-way fixed effects but the regressor of interest is a reversible state indicator or a time-invariant group indicator, not an adoption. Not a DiD under the protocol.
data_statement: No data or code availability statement; visibility data are proprietary from Sistrix and product attributes from the commercial tracker Keepa, and the article points only to an online supplement at https://doi.org/10.1177/00222429251360772.

design: Live-streaming channels on an anonymized platform over 12 weekly periods (Feb 18-May 11, 2020); on March 17, 2020 (start of Period 5) the platform gave all partnered channels the ability to run midroll ads; treated = ever-partnered channels, control = nonpartnered channels, so the main design is a single policy date with treated and control groups.
reason: The primary specification (eq. 2, Table 3) is a two-group single-date DiD: Ti (ever partnered) x Postt (Period >= 5) with channel and period FE plus time-varying categorical controls for language, content category, and target audience, so it is neither staggered nor control-free. The only staggered treatment of the data is a Callaway-Sant'Anna run (Figure 1, prose ATT = .192 and .207 with p-values only) motivated by a 'small portion' of nonpartnered channels that converted to partnered after March 17; it uses a generalized propensity score on covariates and its details are deferred to Web Appendix G, Table W8. Because adoption is essentially a single date for everyone treated and the main spec codes it that way, the paper does not have a staggered binary adoption design under the protocol.
appendix_only_specs: Web Appendix G (Table W8) holds the CSA dynamic ATTs and the SDID details; Web Appendix F adds lagged-DV and stream-count controls; Web Appendix H has PSM/weighting DiD, an attrition sample, and a zero-inflation analysis; Web Appendix I has the COVID-19 and spillover checks (Tables W16-W17); Web Appendices L-O hold the heterogeneity tables (W22-W25).
notes: Borderline between ineligible and near-miss: late partner conversions create a few later adoption dates, and the authors run CSA on that basis, so a reader could label this near-miss (violations: time-varying controls in eq. 2; single-date Ti x Postt coding; propensity-score-adjusted CSA reported only as point estimates and a figure; SDID and PSM excluded). Either way nothing in the main text qualifies: Table 2 is a pre-period placebo, Table 3 the controlled single-date TWFE, Table 4 mechanism outcomes with 'TWFE PSM and weighting', Tables 5-6 subgroup splits with controls. Only 4 pre-periods and 8 post-periods (weekly aggregation). Data come from a third-party agency scraping public APIs and the platform is anonymized; the data overlap the first COVID-19 lockdown.
data_statement: No data or code availability statement; the article gives only an online supplement link (https://doi.org/10.1177/00222429251363144), says the data come from an agency that collects public-API data from live-streaming services, and withholds the platform's identity.

design: Study 1: quarterly customer-level panel from a US fashion retailer, 2008 to 2016 (372,863 customer-quarters; 1,623 customizers, 20,254 never-customizing choosers); treatment is a customer's first customized purchase, which occurs in customer-specific quarters, with choosers as never-treated controls; outcomes are log items purchased, log purchase visits and log spending.

design: 200,455 song-playlist quasi-experiments on Spotify (June 2021-July 2024, daily global streams): treatment = a song being listed on a single curated playlist on song-specific date t0 and delisted on t1 (about 88 days later); each treated song is paired with a one-to-one matched never-(de)listed control song chosen on pre-period stream levels and trends.
reason: Listings occur on unit-specific dates across thousands of playlists, so adoption is staggered and binary, but every main-text specification violates several rules at once. Equations 1 and 3 (Table 3, Models M1 and M2) are explicitly a stacked DiD (the authors cite Cengiz et al. 2019) built on 13-day windows around listing and delisting with song-by-quasi-experiment-by-window FE and quasi-experiment-by-day FE; control songs are selected by Euclidean-distance matching on pre-treatment streams (matching-based DiD); the regression includes the time-varying covariate ln(OtherPlaylistFollowers); and the treatment switches off at delisting, with a separate AfterListing indicator capturing post-switch-off periods. M2 adds moderator-by-treatment interactions. Figure 5's dynamic event study is estimated within the same stacked/matched framework.
appendix_only_specs: Web Appendix E (placebo tests, delisting-window estimates), H (stricter noise thresholds, including transition days, first-listing subsamples, weighted least squares), I (decay and longer delisting windows); all are variants of the same stacked matched model.
notes: Only main-text coefficient values: M1 beta1 = .077 (SE .001), beta2 = .012 (SE .001); M2 beta1 = .082 (SE .004), beta2 = .039 (SE .005), N = 8,018,200, SEs clustered at song-quasi-experiment-window. There is no unstacked panel TWFE anywhere. Data are proprietary (Soundcharts plus a cooperation partner), so re-estimation is not feasible regardless.
data_statement: A Data Availability section states that an alternative disclosure plan was approved: 'The data that support the findings of this article are not available due to a non-disclosure agreement; however, code and disguised data were shared with the Editor in Chief.' design: Units are market-retailer-category-competing-brand-week cells (NielsenIQ RMS 2010-2019); treatment is the deletion of a national brand from a category at that market-retailer, which rolls out sequentially across DMAs and retailers (1,046 deleted brands, 14,462 market-retailer-deleted-brand cases); controls are the same competing brand at the same retailer in not-yet-treated markets, matched on pre-period correlation >= .8.
reason: The adoption event (brand deletion) is binary and staggered across markets and retailers, so the design is in scope, but every main-text specification violates the protocol. Equations 1-3 (Tables 6, 7, 10) use a stacked DID with matched not-yet-treated controls (correlation threshold), a continuous TreatPost variable equal to the fraction of the deletion completed (0 to 1 ramp, Table 3), control-function/IV terms for deletion timing and marketing mix with Hausman-style instruments, time-varying marketing-mix and competitor-price controls, and moderator-by-TreatPost interactions. No main-text column reports a plain binary-treatment TWFE without these elements.
appendix_only_specs: Web Appendix N reports a Gardner et al. (2024) two-stage DID robustness check and Web Appendix J re-estimates Equation 1 without control-function terms; both retain the stacked matched structure, continuous TreatPost, and marketing-mix controls, so neither would qualify. Web Appendix I has a DID on new-brand launch rates (no details in main text).
notes: Treatment is conceptually a binary deletion but is operationalized as a continuous ramp (1 - Distribution_t/Distribution_T0) during the deletion window (average 22 weeks; 30% complete within one week), reaching 1 at completion. Classified near-miss rather than ineligible because the underlying adoption is a discrete staggered event; a reader who treats the ramp as a continuous treatment could instead call it ineligible. Standard errors clustered at retailer-category-deleted brand-competing brand.
data_statement: Data Availability section states the NielsenIQ RMS data are from the Kilts Center for Marketing, used under license and not publicly available; available from the corresponding author on reasonable request with Kilts permission. design: Firm-year panel of 925 Compustat firms 1995-2018; binary treatment = state court recognition of the inevitable disclosure doctrine in the firm's headquarters state (lagged one year), staggered across five treated states (Georgia 1998, Ohio 2000, plus Kansas, Missouri, Utah at other dates); controls are firms in 28 states that never recognized the IDD; treatment switches off for Georgia (2013) and Ohio (2008) after rejection.
reason: The design is a textbook staggered binary TWFE (Eq. 1, firm and year FE) and the authors call it a staggered DiD, but every main-text specification includes the lagged time-varying control vector (sales, leverage, ROA, TMT size, analyst following, institutional ownership, industry competition/growth, state GDP growth, unemployment) plus an inverse Mills ratio from a first-stage disclosure probit. Table 2 Models 1-6, Table 3, Table 4 Models 1a-6b, Table 5, and Table 6 all carry these controls; no main-text column reports the TWFE without controls. Table 2 Model 7 is a stacked DiD (excluded anyway), and the relative-time event study (Eq. 4) is reported only in Web Appendix A8, also with controls.

A20: state-level regressions.
notes: Treatment is lagged (IDD_{g,t-1}) and switches off for Georgia and Ohio after rejection, coded 0 (Chen et al. 2022 convention); a re-estimation would need to drop post-rejection periods. design: HKTVmall customers (user-week panel, Oct 2019-Nov 2020, 58 weeks); treatment = first self-pickup station opening within 400 m of the customer's residence, 40 station openings collapsed into 16 distinct treatment weeks; never-treated controls = customers with no station within 400 m by the end of the study period.
reason: The design is staggered binary adoption with never-treated controls (Identification Strategy section, Table 2, footnote 9: 16 distinct treatment times). But every main-text specification violates a rule: Tables 3, 4, 7-9 columns 1-4, and 11-13 are Synthetic DiD (Arkhangelsky et al. 2021, Equations 1-2) with the outcome residualized on customer-time-specific Delivery Fee Scheme dummies (Equations 3-4), i.e. synthetic DiD plus time-varying controls. The only TWFE regressions (Table 6; Tables 7, 8, 9 column 5) use a Pareto/NBD model-derived logit churn probability as outcome, include the same time-varying Delivery Fee Scheme controls, and in Tables 7-9 add subgroup-by-treatment triple interactions.
appendix_only_specs: Web Appendix I (Table W8) re-estimates the main effect by static TWFE (user FE + week FE) and Equation W2 is an unstacked event study with relative-time bins, but both include the time-varying Delivery Fee Scheme dummies X_it; Table W9 adds moderator interactions; Web Appendix M (Equation W3) is an event study for churn, also with the controls; Web Appendix N Table W13 column 5 is TWFE on interpurchase duration with controls. None is a clean no-controls TWFE.
notes: Author Accepted Manuscript with reviewer line numbers interleaved in the text extraction. The paper itself calls the setting a staggered adoption design and cites Athey-Imbens 2022 and Clarke et al. 2023. Delivery Fee Scheme dummies are described in Web Appendix A as customer-time-specific (membership tier x fee-regime revisions), so they are genuinely time-varying controls, not absorbed by week FE. Treatment is an absorbing state (first station access), so no switch-off issue. No estimator-comparison literature (Goodman-Bacon, CSA) is cited.
data_statement: Data Availability Statement: an alternative disclosure plan was approved; the data supporting the findings are not available, but simulated data are posted in Harvard Dataverse (https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/XHW6DH), with results on simulated data stated to differ numerically from the paper.

design: US public firms (Compustat/BoardEx, 2000-2019) that experience a CEO death or severe illness; treatment is a binary 'marketing CEO' (any marketing experience) taking over after the death, which occurs at firm-specific years; comparison group is not described (presumably not-yet- or never-treated firms, or firms with non-marketing successors).
reason: The main hypothesis tests (Table 5, Models 1-4, eq. 2-3) use a continuous marketing-CEO share-of-career measure, ~20 time-varying firm/CEO controls, and control-function first-stage residuals plus inverse Mills ratio terms, so they fail the continuous-treatment, time-varying-controls, and IV rules. Table 4 is a pre/post mean comparison of differentiation five years before vs after the death with no comparison group and no regression. The only candidate spec is the staggered Callaway-Sant'Anna DiD reported in prose (p. 38, fn. 5-6) and plotted in Figure 3: binary incoming-marketing-CEO treatment at staggered death dates, ATT = .106, p = .021. Because CSA is explicitly reported and I cannot identify a violated rule from what is printed, the protocol classifies it as eligible, but the specification is too sparsely described to be sure.

design: Firm-year panel of 123-155 publicly traded US firms, 2000-2011 (Samples 1-4); binary treatment is CMO presence in the top management team, which switches on (and often off) at firm-specific years (63% of Sample 4 firms switch at least once), with never-CMO firms (30%) and always-CMO firms (7%) as comparison.
reason: The fixed-effects model (Model 4, Eq. 4) in Table 5 and Table 6 is a TWFE regression of Tobin's q on the binary CMO indicator with firm and year fixed effects, so the design is staggered and binary. However, every main-text specification (Tables 5-8, footnote a) includes the full N&M set of time-varying controls (innovation, differentiation, diversification, CEO tenure, outsider CEO, market concentration, log employees, COO presence, ROA, sales growth), and no column is reported without controls. The other models are OLS, between-effects, random-effects, lagged-DV, 2SLS-IV, control function, Hausman-Taylor and Blundell-Bond GMM, all excluded by the protocol.
appendix_only_specs: Web Appendix Tables WA5-WA7 report the full model results (same nine models, same controls) for Samples 1-3; no controls-free TWFE there either, judging from the description in the text.
notes: The paper is not framed as DiD; it is a panel regression of a strategic choice variable. CMO presence frequently reverses (many firms switch more than once), so the 'drop post-adoption zeros' rule would discard a large share of observations; treatment also includes firms that start treated in 2000. Table 5 footnote b reports an OLS (no firm FE) variant with industry-by-year FE. design: Customer-week panel (170 weeks, Jan 2008-Mar 2011) of a wine-and-spirits retailer's loyalty-card customers; treatment = the customer joining the firm's social media page and thereby receiving firm-generated content, with join dates staggered across 412 treated customers (Figure 2); comparison = 412 never-participating customers selected by 1:1 nearest-neighbor propensity-score matching.
reason: The FGC_iht indicator switches on at each treated customer's own join date (footnote 6, Figure 2), so the design is staggered and binary with never-treated controls. But every main-text specification violates the rules: the control group is constructed by propensity-score matching (matching-based DiD); the DID model in Equations 1-4 and Table 3 (M1-M5) has pair-level intercepts a0ih but no calendar-week fixed effects, and M2-M5 add time-varying controls (TVAd, Email, CExp, PromD/CrossP), triple interactions with customer characteristics, AR(1) errors, and a Type I Tobit (nonlinear) in M5, all estimated by hierarchical Bayes MCMC; Table 5 repeats this for profit. The TE model (Equations 5-7, Tables 4, 6) is a selection model on post-period data only with continuous FGC intensity.
appendix_only_specs: Web Appendices W1-W13 cover sample construction, PSM diagnostics, survey constructs, MCMC details and elasticity calculations; no additional regression specification is described, and robustness variants (alternative post period, random instead of matched controls, outlier removal) are 'available from the authors on request'.
notes: Even the benchmark 'standard DID' column M1 in Table 3 (TCust, FGC, TCust x FGC) has no unit or week fixed effects, so there is no TWFE anywhere in the paper. Treatment is customer self-selection into the firm's page rather than an externally timed rollout. Cites Angrist-Pischke 2009 and Huang et al. 2012 for the PSM-DiD approach; no modern staggered-DiD literature. Published JM 2016, 80(1), 7-25.
data_statement: No data or code availability statement; data are proprietary loyalty-card, social media participation, and survey data from an unnamed specialty retailer (social media platform name withheld for confidentiality), with an Online Supplement at http://dx.doi.org/10.1509/jm.14.0249 and additional results 'available from the authors on request'.

design: Customers of a U.S. B2B electrical-components distributor; treatment = the customer's sales rep departs (voluntary turnover) and the account is reassigned, at rep-specific departure dates spread across 2011 (129 reps); 830 treated customers versus 1,615 stratified-random control customers whose reps never departed; outcome is log annual sales one year before versus one year after the departure date.
reason: Underlying adoption is staggered and binary with never-treated controls, but the article collapses the panel into two event-time periods (T1 = year before, T2 = year after the departure date) and estimates Eq. 1-5 as 2x2 DiD regressions with a treatment-group dummy, a relative-time Post dummy, and their interaction, using customer random effects rather than unit fixed effects and departure-quarter dummies rather than calendar-time fixed effects. Table 7 Column 1 (coef -.193, SE .053) is the only controls-free column but it is this two-period event-time collapse without unit or calendar-time FE; Columns 2-5 add time-varying customer and rep covariates, branch and industry FE, and a Heckman inverse Mills ratio. Tables 9 (matching), 10, 11 (ten-quarter window) and 12 share these features.
appendix_only_specs: Web Appendix: two-quarter window versions of the DiD and PSM estimates, subsample matching results for new-hire vs existing-rep reassignments, robustness with sales volatility and peer-dissimilarity controls, lagged unemployment instruments. All appear to use the same two-period collapse.
notes: The authors explicitly cite Bertrand, Duflo, and Mullainathan (2004) as the reason for collapsing to two periods. A replicator could in principle rebuild a customer-quarter staggered panel from the 2008-2013 transaction data, but no such specification is reported. Verdict could be read as ineligible if the lead requires a calendar-time panel regression to appear in the article; I classify it as near-miss because the adoption design itself is staggered and binary and 'two-period collapse' is a listed near-miss reason. Treatment never switches off.
data_statement: Proprietary customer-level transaction and HR data from an unnamed leading U.S. distributor of electrical component products (a Fortune 500 firm); no data or code availability statement; an online supplement/web appendix is at http://dx.doi.org/10.1509/jm.15.0358.

design: Daily e-book prices for about 2,000 New York Times best-seller titles at Amazon and Barnes & Noble, Jan 2012-Dec 2013; binary treatment = the title's publisher has switched from the agency model back to the (modified) wholesale model so the retailer sets the price, with six Big Six publishers switching at five distinct dates (Harper Collins 9/10/2012, Hachette 12/4/2012, Simon & Schuster 12/17/2012, Macmillan 4/4/2013, Penguin and Random House 9/1/2013); comparison units are not-yet-switched Big Six titles in the main sample and never-treated non-Big-Six titles in a robustness row.
reason: The design is a staggered binary adoption with publisher (group) or book fixed effects and week fixed effects (Section 4.1 specification; Table 3), and treatment never switches off. However, every main-text column includes time-varying book controls: ln(daily sales rank), cumulative number of Amazon reviews, and years since release are retained even in the book-fixed-effects columns of Table 3 (coefficients -0.024, -0.025, -0.193 at Amazon), which confirms they vary within title over time. Tables 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11 and 14 all state they include 'controls as the main specification in Table 3', Table 4 adds publisher-specific trends, Table 6 windowed columns are single-publisher regressions, and Table 9 is a synthetic control; no column reports the TWFE without controls.
appendix_only_specs: none (the article has no appendix).
notes: Would be eligible if a controls-free column existed: Table 3 book-FE Amazon coefficient -0.191 (SE 0.006), Barnes & Noble -0.077 (0.007); publisher-FE columns -0.199 (0.006) and -0.088 (0.007); SEs clustered by book. The main sample contains only eventually-treated Big Six titles (identification from not-yet-treated units through Sep 2013); Table 5 'Including other publishers' adds never-treated titles (-0.233 and -0.108). Table 5 'Residualized two-period panel' follows Bertrand et al. (2004) two-step aggregation. Treatment dating uses Amazon's price-setter label; other retailers assumed to switch within days.
data_statement: Data were collected by the authors with a web scraper from Amazon, Barnes & Noble, Books-A-Million and Apple during 2012-2013; no data or code availability statement and no repository is mentioned; NET Institute funding acknowledged.

design: FP-country-year panel of Kiva field partners (771 observations, 155 FPs in 63 countries, 2008 to 2012); treatment is the entry of the intermediary-free platform Zidisha into a country, which happened in 10 countries at different months between October 2009 and 2012, with Kiva FPs in the other 53 countries as never-treated controls; outcomes are log average APR, log percent of loans delinquent and log percent of loans funded.
reason: Table 4 Columns 4 and 7 are labelled Diff-in-Diff and regress log delinquency rate and log funding rate on a Zidisha presence dummy with field-partner, country and year fixed effects (Column 1, the IV first stage, is the same regression with log APR as outcome; Table 5 Column 2 likewise). Every one of these columns also includes time-varying FP-country-year controls (log banks per 100K residents, log number of FPs in the country-year, log average loan term, log average loan size, loan size over GDP per capita, average number of borrowers, female borrower share, share with English description, log GDP per capita), which the protocol excludes, and no column is reported without them. Columns 2, 3, 5 and 6 of Table 4 and Table 5 Columns 1 and 3 use the continuous log APR as the regressor (OLS and 2SLS), so they are not binary-treatment DiDs.
appendix_only_specs: Appendix E (Table 6) compares Kiva loan characteristics before and after Zidisha entry descriptively; Appendix D reports simulations. The text mentions that a regression discontinuity analysis gives comparable results but does not report it.
notes: Staggered binary entry with many never-treated countries, so the design itself fits the protocol; the obstacle is the time-varying controls in every column. Printed Zidisha dummy coefficients: Table 4 Column 1 (log APR) -0.096 (0.014); Column 4 (log delinquency) -0.094 (0.009); Column 7 (log funded) 0.005 (0.004); Table 5 Column 2 (log APR, with log loans in other markets) -0.101 (0.015). FP and country fixed effects are both included although FPs are mostly country-specific. The paper is primarily an analytical model of field-partner incentives; the DiD is a robustness exercise.
data_statement: No data or code availability statement; Kiva data were scraped by the authors, historical APRs taken from the Wayback Machine, local financial data from the World Bank Global Financial Development Database, and Zidisha loan data collected from that platform.

design: Brand-month panel of 538 U.S. national brands (Jan 2007-Jun 2013) relating log TV and Internet advertising dollars to log word-of-mouth mentions; a second analysis treats being a Super Bowl advertiser (binary, same February date every year) with generalized synthetic control.
reason: The main model (Eq. 1, Tables 2 and 3) regresses log WOM on continuous log advertising expenditures with brand fixed effects, category-quarter-year fixed effects, two lagged dependent variables, news mentions, and brand random coefficients; there is no binary adoption treatment. The Super Bowl analysis (Section 6.2, Table 4, Fig. 3) uses Xu's (2017) generalized synthetic control on brand/Super-Bowl-year units where all treated units are treated at the same calendar event, so it is neither staggered nor a TWFE regression. Table 3 adds a Super Bowl dummy to the continuous-advertising model with lagged WOM and interactions, which is not a DiD design.
appendix_only_specs: none relevant; Web Appendix 3 (Tables 10-12) reports nested specifications and 2SLS/Lasso-IV versions of the continuous advertising model, and Web Appendix 2 adds lagged advertising.
notes: Treatment of interest is continuous advertising spending; the only binary treatment (Super Bowl advertiser) is estimated by synthetic control with a common event date and interactive fixed effects. Web appendices are printed inside the article text file.
data_statement: Data come from proprietary sources (Keller Fay TalkTrack WOM panel, Nielsen-McKinsey Insight online posts, Kantar Media Ad$pender, LexisNexis); no data or code repository is mentioned; some alternative results are said to be 'available from the authors'. Article is open access (CC BY 4.0).

design: Two panels, 2010-2019 annual: (a) Circana household-year panel where treatment = a dollar store chain entry within 0-2 miles (or 2-5 miles) of the household's census tract, with 14,554 entries staggered across tracts and never-entered tracts as controls; (b) census-tract-year panel where treatment = dollar store entry in the tract (0-2 mi radius), outcome = number of independent grocery stores, with tract FE and county-by-year FE and never-entered tracts as controls.
reason: The paper explicitly describes the design as 'a Difference-in-Difference with a staggered roll-out of treatment', cites Goodman-Bacon and Sun-Abraham, and reports Callaway-Sant'Anna event studies alongside TWFE (Figures 3, 5, 6). But no main-text specification is clean: the static Equations 1 and 3 (Tables 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9) code treatment as a categorical count of entries (One / Two / Three+ DS entries) rather than a binary indicator, and every table and both event-study equations (Eq. 2 with beta*X_it household demographics; Eq. 4 with beta*X_lbt local population, income, rents, their growth rates, and business density) include time-varying controls. Table 7 column 1 (tract FE + year FE) still includes demographic controls. The event-study figures print no coefficients.
appendix_only_specs: Appendix A: Fig. 7 (grocery-store event study with TWFE, Borusyak-Jaravel-Spiess, Sun-Abraham, and CSA), Fig. 8 (fresh-produce event study with the same four estimators), Fig. 9 (event studies by reporting-weeks subsample), Table 12 (other store types), Table 13 (robustness: no nearby entry; excluding never-treated), Table 14 (fresh produce ounces). All inherit the time-varying controls of Equations 2 and 4; none prints event-study coefficients.
notes: Closest-to-eligible item is the binary-entry event study (Eq. 2 / Eq. 4) estimated by CSA in Figures 3, 5, 6, but the equations include time-varying covariates and the figure captions list only household/tract and year FE, so the controls cannot be ruled out; confidence is medium for that reason. County-by-year FE in the tract panel would be allowed on its own. Treatment is absorbing (entry 'has occurred by t'), so no switch-off problem. Household treatment is defined at the tract level with multiple entries possible. If the lead treats CSA-with-covariates figures as acceptable, this paper would need the coefficient values, which are not printed anywhere in the article.
data_statement: Data Availability statement: 'Some data was provided by the USDA under a Third Party Agreement with Circana. All other data will be provided as supplementary information files.' The SNAP Retailer panel and Census/ACS data are public; the Circana Consumer Network household panel is restricted; no code repository is named.
